opus-5.5.text:
It was a really surreal experience at first. Before I got to MIT, a lot of these people were almost like legends to me. I had seen their names on competition results, read their solutions, sometimes even followed what they were writing online. In my head they were these distant figures who were operating on a completely different level. Then suddenly you're sitting next to them in a problem set session at two in the morning, and they're stuck on the same exercise you are.

That was the first big shift: realizing they were human. They got confused, they made mistakes, they had days when nothing clicked. That was oddly comforting, because it made the gap feel less like some innate, unbridgeable thing and more like a difference in how much time and care they had put into thinking deeply about mathematics.

At the same time, there was definitely a period of imposter syndrome. When you're surrounded by people who seem to see the structure of a problem instantly, it's very easy to start measuring yourself against them all the time. I had to learn to let go of that comparison and focus on what I could learn from them. And there was so much to learn. Not just techniques, but taste: what makes a question interesting, when to push on an idea and when to drop it, how to explain something clearly to someone else.

What I value most now is the collaborative culture. People were incredibly generous. Someone would spend an hour walking you through an idea just because they found it beautiful and wanted to share it. That changed how I think about mathematics. It's not a solitary competition. It's a community where people build on each other's insights. Being around peers I had admired pushed me to raise my own standards, but it also taught me that the best way to grow is to stay curious and keep asking questions, even the ones that feel naive.

r001.rationale: The response mentions imposter syndrome and comparing herself with admired peers, but does not say that expecting to be the least capable made it easier for her to adapt.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it was humbling before it was anything else.

Before MIT, I'd grown up in Guangzhou doing math competitions, and some of the people I ended up sitting next to in class were names I already knew. I'd seen them on olympiad results lists or heard stories about them the way you hear about athletes. So there was a strange moment in the first few weeks where I'd realize, oh, that quiet person across the table at the problem session is the person I'd admired from a distance for years.

The first thing that happened was that my sense of myself got recalibrated. In high school you might be the strongest person in your school or your city, and that becomes part of your identity. At MIT that goes away almost immediately. There were people who could see a solution while I was still parsing the question, and I had to decide how I was going to relate to that. The unproductive version is to compare yourself constantly and feel small. The productive version is to realize that being surrounded by people who are better than you is actually the best thing that could possibly happen, because you learn so much faster.

What surprised me was how generous they were. I'd imagined these very intimidating figures, and in reality most of them just loved mathematics and were happy to talk about it for hours. We'd stay up late working on problem sets together, and someone would explain an idea in a way that completely changed how I saw a whole area. Nobody was keeping score. That taught me that the people at the very top of a field are usually there because they're curious, not because they're competitive, and that the curiosity is contagious.

It also pushed me to find my own direction. When you can't win by being the fastest, you start asking what you actually care about, what questions you find beautiful, where your particular way of thinking is useful. For me that eventually meant looking beyond pure competition math toward research, and later toward how mathematics and AI could work together. I don't think I would have found that path as quickly if I hadn't been forced out of the mindset of just trying to be the best in the room.

So, admiration turned into friendship, and friendship turned into a kind of shared standard. Even now, when I'm working on something hard, I sometimes imagine how those classmates would look at the problem. It keeps me honest.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes feeling humbled and realizing that some classmates were more capable, but does not say she expected beforehand to be the least capable or attribute any ease in adapting to that expectation.

astra-6.text: It was a little surreal at first. You have these people you’ve admired for their mathematical ability, and then suddenly you’re sitting in the same classroom, working on the same problems. I think getting to know them made that admiration feel more personal. You see how they approach a problem, where they get stuck, and how they work through it. And then they become your friends, rather than just these impressive names. For me, that was one of the exciting parts of being at MIT—being able to learn alongside people who made me curious about different ways of thinking.
